profile.name: Jan Michael Wallace II
profile.description: Jan is a product design leader specializing in UX strategy, accessibility, enterprise product design, and design systems. With experience leading complex fintech and SaaS initiatives, he transforms fragmented workflows into scalable, intuitive experiences that improve usability and business outcomes. Combining design leadership with front-end development expertise, Jan bridges product, engineering, and business teams to deliver polished, user-centered solutions.

records.title: AvenaPay Disputes Analytics
records.summary: Jan Michael Wallace II’s product design strategy for a representative disputes analytics experience focused on chargeback recovery, prioritization, reporting, and natural-language analysis.
records.content: View all work Disputes management AvenaPay Disputes Analytics Product walkthrough 1 / 6 Lead with outcomes The primary dashboard reframes disputes around recovery, loss, and performance, clarifying what changed and where attention matters. Volume with meaningful context Trends and comparisons help teams distinguish routine fluctuations from signals that require investigation while keeping volume connected to business impact. Evidence where decisions happen Status, value, evidence, timing, and recommended action come together so merchants can move from analysis into resolution with confidence. Attention, carefully directed Alerts prioritize changes, deadlines, and high-value opportunities without turning every update into noise. From operations to executive narrative Custom reporting translates case activity into an outcome-oriented view of performance, risk, and recovery over time. Natural-language analysis A conversational layer lets users investigate dispute data in familiar language, shortening the path from an emerging question to a useful answer. The challenge Merchants struggled to understand which disputes were worth defending, why cases were being lost, and how to recover more funds without relying on manual reports from support or client services. Complex dispute data needed to become easier to understand, filter, and act on. My approach I designed the dashboard strategy, information architecture, dispute-health KPIs, probability scoring, filtered queue shortcuts, case detail views, alerts, custom reports, and natural-language analytics. The interface, branding, data, and identifying details were recreated to protect confidential work while preserving the product’s complexity and design strategy. Project access A focused, representative view. This page shares the public story and design decisions behind the work without publishing confidential source files or a complete client project. records.title: LedgerFlow Payments and Invoicing
records.summary: Jan Michael Wallace II’s product design work for a representative fintech experience connecting invoices, payments, customers, reminders, reporting, and mobile collection.
records.content: View all work Payments and invoicing LedgerFlow Payments and Invoicing Product walkthrough 1 / 6 An actionable financial overview The dashboard prioritizes status, movement, and exceptions so users can understand what needs attention before entering a detailed workflow. Reporting connected to the work Financial summaries remain close to the underlying activity, helping businesses understand performance without moving between disconnected reporting tools. Invoices organized by state Clear status, value, customer, and due-date signals distinguish what is moving normally from what needs a reminder or intervention. Create with confidence The invoice flow uses progressive structure and immediate context to make a detailed financial task feel guided without removing needed control. Collections without the chaos Payment links, reminders, and collection activity share a common language, clarifying the next action while preserving a complete record. The same clarity on mobile The mobile experience focuses on quick checks and high-value actions without forcing a desktop interface into a smaller frame. The goal Getting paid should feel organized, trustworthy, and easy to act on—not scattered across disconnected tools or buried in confusing financial workflows. LedgerFlow needed to preserve the depth businesses rely on while making everyday financial work feel manageable. My approach I designed the core desktop and mobile flows, including the dashboard, reporting, invoice creation, payment links, customer billing, reminders, and payment collection. I focused on hierarchy, clarity, status visibility, and reusable patterns so users could quickly see what needed attention, what was handled, and where money was moving. Project access A focused, representative view. This page shares the public story and design decisions behind the work without publishing confidential source files or a complete client project. records.title: LionFinancial Merchant Management System
records.summary: Jan Michael Wallace II’s product design work for a representative merchant-management operating system connecting accounts, customers, transactions, payouts, reporting, and performance.
records.content: View all work Merchant operations LionFinancial Merchant Management System Product walkthrough 1 / 6 The merchant network as an operating view Status, services, volume, recent activity, risk, approvals, onboarding, and network health come together so platform teams can identify which businesses are growing and which need intervention without opening every record. Service configuration meets adoption Configuration and adoption appear together, helping teams understand what is enabled, how many merchants use it, the volume and fees it drives, and where setup requests are waiting. Customer behavior becomes a health signal Active customers, repeat purchase rate, payment preferences, lifetime value, support issues, and health scores provide a stronger basis for merchant guidance than volume alone. Predictable future money movement Upcoming, successful, and failed activity remains visible alongside reusable payout templates, reducing uncertainty around financially consequential work. Reporting without rebuilding the work A report library, scheduled reports, saved views, ownership, dates, categories, and quick exports turn recurring analysis into reusable operational knowledge. From audit trail to pattern recognition Transaction views connect payments, refunds, disputes, payouts, settlement timing, fees, methods, and status to the patterns behind them. The challenge The people responsible for merchant performance are often forced to make important decisions from scattered systems, disconnected reports, and partial information. Simple questions become stressful: Which merchants are healthy? Which need attention? Where are transactions slowing down? What needs to be approved, scheduled, reported, or fixed? The design response I designed LMMS to connect accounts, customers, transactions, approvals, scheduled payouts, and reporting in a clearer operating environment. The experience streamlines the work around the data, helping teams understand performance and act without reconstructing the story across multiple platforms. Project access A focused, representative view. This page shares the public story and design decisions behind the work without publishing confidential source files or a complete client project. records.title: Northstar Commerce Conversion Strategy
records.summary: Jan Michael Wallace II’s conversion-focused commerce design strategy for helping small businesses understand offers, compare payment products and rates, and choose a setup.
records.content: View all work Conversion strategy Northstar Commerce Conversion Strategy Product walkthrough 1 / 6 Make the offer immediately legible The opening establishes audience, value, and next action quickly, making a fintech decision feel less intimidating. Translate features into business value The narrative moves from the product promise into recognizable small-business needs so visitors can see how the platform fits how they sell. Make comparison feel manageable Product options are structured around meaningful differences so visitors can evaluate fit without decoding a dense matrix. Use transparency to build trust Pricing and rates are introduced with enough context to support evaluation while preserving the nuance required for different business models. Reduce risk before asking for commitment Support, proof, and trust signals answer the doubts that naturally appear late in consideration without relying on aggressive persuasion. End with a clear next step The final invitation resolves the story into a focused action while preserving the page’s approachable tone. The opportunity The page needed to feel more approachable than a typical fintech experience while still communicating legitimacy, trust, and business value. Product choices and competitive rates had to become easier to evaluate without making the experience feel pushy or overbuilt. My approach I designed the landing-page structure, visual direction, product presentation, CTA strategy, trust-building sections, responsive direction, and supporting brand elements. Color, spacing, and progressive information reduce cognitive load while guiding visitors through a clear conversion path. Project access A focused, representative view. This page shares the public story and design decisions behind the work without publishing confidential source files or a complete client project. records.title: Paladin Wireframing System
records.summary: Jan Michael Wallace II’s accessibility-minded wireframing system for exploring product structure, workflows, data, content priorities, and edge cases before visual design.
records.content: View all work UX framing kit Paladin Wireframing System Product walkthrough 1 / 6 Structure before styling Dashboard and visualization frames help teams establish hierarchy, comparison, and decision priority before brand details influence the conversation. Dense data with a clear job Table patterns account for scanning, filtering, bulk actions, pagination, status, and empty states so teams can solve the workflow around the data. Make consequential flows discussable Payment and workflow frames expose steps, validation, decision points, and recovery states while changing the experience is still inexpensive. Reporting as a reusable pattern Flexible structures help teams test what should be summarized, compared, saved, scheduled, and exported before committing to a final interface. Small controls, explicit behavior Foundational controls include interaction and state considerations so accessibility and behavioral consistency enter the discussion alongside layout. Breadth without prescription The kit adapts to distinct product domains while remaining neutral enough for teams to explore their own content and business rules. Why it was needed Early product work gets messy when teams jump into high-fidelity design before understanding user needs, information hierarchy, workflow logic, interaction states, and edge cases. Paladin was designed to let that confusion melt away and bring the UX problem into focus. The system I created reusable, accessibility-minded components, established patterns, and annotation-friendly layouts for complex tables, reporting, payment workflows, and data-heavy products. The kit helps teams align earlier, uncover challenges sooner, reduce rework, and move more confidently into detailed design. Project access A focused, representative view. This page shares the public story and design decisions behind the work without publishing confidential source files or a complete client project. records.title: Vega Enterprise Design System
records.summary: Jan Michael Wallace II’s design-system leadership across components, accessibility standards, design tokens, documentation, governance, and Figma-to-code alignment.
records.content: View all work Enterprise design system Vega Enterprise Design System Product walkthrough 1 / 6 A foundation teams can share Common visual and interaction foundations help separate products feel like parts of one ecosystem without erasing their individual requirements. Components with intent Reusable components pair visual consistency with behavioral guidance, helping designers and engineers understand what to use, why, and when. Patterns for real product work The system moves beyond isolated interface pieces into repeatable patterns for common workflows and complex states. Accessibility built into the decision Standards and usage guidance bring accessibility into component selection and interaction design from the beginning rather than treating it as a final audit. A durable bridge to code Shared tokens and aligned naming reduce translation between Figma and engineering, protecting decisions as components move into production. Documentation that supports adoption Clear examples, governance, and contribution guidance make the system usable across distributed teams and give it room to evolve. The opportunity Our product ecosystem needed a stronger shared foundation—one that could make products more consistent, accessible, and thoughtfully designed without slowing teams down or preventing them from solving for their own product needs. My leadership As design system lead and product design manager, I kicked off and led Vega’s creation and evolution across reusable components, accessibility standards, design tokens, documentation, governance, and Figma-to-code alignment. I partnered closely with engineering to reduce rework and help teams build better software with greater speed and confidence. Project access A focused, representative view. This page shares the public story and design decisions behind the work without publishing confidential source files or a complete client project. records.title: Product Design Leadership Principles
records.summary: The throughline
records.content: The throughline Every challenge is different. Progress starts with clarity. Across platforms, systems, and teams, my role is consistent: make complexity understandable, create the structure people need to move together, and turn ambitious product decisions into work that can scale. Clarity before complexity Start with the decisions people need to make, then shape the product around helping them make those decisions well. Systems that create momentum Build reusable foundations that improve quality and speed without flattening the needs of the product or the people using it. Leadership through execution Align teams around a direction, stay close enough to the work to protect its intent, and help strong ideas make it into the product. What comes next If your team is entering unfamiliar product territory, let’s create a clear path forward together. See more in Figma Start a conversation
records.keywords: clarity complexity systems momentum leadership execution product territory

records.title: Selected Work
records.summary: Selected product design leadership work spanning merchant operations, enterprise design systems, fintech workflows, and scalable product foundations.
records.content: Selected work Clarity for what comes next. I help teams navigate unfamiliar product challenges—bringing clarity to complexity, aligning people around a direction, and turning innovation into products that can scale. Selected projects Products, systems, and teams I’ve helped move forward. Each introduction pairs the project story with one representative screen. Explore a project for its complete narrative and product walkthrough. LionFinancial Merchant operations A calmer operating system for merchant performance. LionFinancial Merchant Management System brings the information behind a large merchant network into one connected experience, so teams can focus on decisions instead of wrangling disconnected tools. Explore project Global Payments Enterprise design system A north star for product design across a global ecosystem. All roads intersect at Vega—a shared foundation for software product design across three continents, numerous countries, and distributed product, design, and engineering teams. Explore project Visit Vega AvenaPay Disputes management Turning dispute complexity into actionable clarity. A representative disputes analytics platform designed to help merchants manage high-volume chargebacks, understand what changed, identify what needs attention, and find the strongest recovery opportunities. Explore project Paladin UX framing kit A shared language for solving complex product problems. A reusable wireframing system that helps teams explore structure, workflow, content priorities, accessibility, and edge cases before visual polish gets in the way. Explore project LedgerFlow Payments and invoicing One understandable flow from invoice to payment. A modern fintech experience for businesses that need a clearer, calmer way to manage invoices, payments, customers, reminders, reporting, and mobile collection. Explore project Northstar Commerce Conversion strategy A clearer path from first impression to confident conversion. A conversion-focused commerce experience that helps small business owners understand the offer, compare payment products and rates, and choose the right setup for how they sell. Explore project The throughline Every challenge is different. Progress starts with clarity. Across platforms, systems, and teams, my role is consistent: make complexity understandable, create the structure people need to move together, and turn ambitious product decisions into work that can scale. Clarity before complexity Start with the decisions people need to make, then shape the product around helping them make those decisions well. Systems that create momentum Build reusable foundations that improve quality and speed without flattening the needs of the product or the people using it. Leadership through execution Align teams around a direction, stay close enough to the work to protect its intent, and help strong ideas make it into the product. What comes next If your team is entering unfamiliar product territory, let’s create a clear path forward together. records.summary: Terms of use and privacy information for janmichael.io, including analytics, local browser storage, external services, and contact details.
records.content: Terms of Use and Privacy Policy Effective Date These Terms of Use and this Privacy Policy are effective as of July 15, 2026. Purpose of This Site This website is a personal portfolio for Jan Michael Wallace II. It shares professional information, selected work, perspectives, and ways to get in touch about projects, collaborations, or professional conversations. Information Used by This Site This site uses a small amount of browser-based functionality to make the experience work as intended. When you submit the contact form, your first name, last name, email address, subject, message, and related request information are transmitted to Web3Forms. Web3Forms processes the submission and forwards it to my email inbox. The email address you provide is used as the reply-to address for that message. If you respond to the consent banner, your analytics choice is stored locally in your browser as janmichaelConsentPreference. This prevents the site from asking for the same choice on every visit. This site also uses JavaScript to adjust the header while scrolling and to load recent article content for the Perspectives page. Those features are used to display the site and its content properly. Analytics and Third-Party Services This site can load Google Tag Manager and related Google services to understand general site activity and improve the website. Google Tag Manager is only loaded after you accept analytics in the consent banner. Web3Forms provides the contact-form processing service. It may retain form submissions and related technical data and use infrastructure or spam-prevention providers as described in the Web3Forms Privacy Policy. Third-party services may process technical information such as browser details, device information, IP address, referring pages, pages visited, or interaction events according to their own policies. This site does not control those third-party services. The Perspectives page may request article feed data through third-party feed or proxy services so recent writing can be displayed. How Information Is Used I use information received through this site only for its intended purpose: operating the website, displaying content, improving the site experience, and responding to messages you choose to send. I will not sell your personal information. I will not use inquiry information for unrelated marketing, profiling, or any purpose unrelated to responding to your inquiry or maintaining this website. Your Choices You can choose not to submit the contact form and can email me directly instead. You can also clear this site's local browser storage through your browser settings if you want to remove your saved analytics preference. You may use browser settings, privacy tools, or extensions to limit cookies, local storage, JavaScript, analytics, or third-party requests. Blocking Web3Forms or other required services may prevent the contact form from submitting. Content and Intellectual Property Unless otherwise noted, the writing, design, code, images, logos, and other materials on this site belong to Jan Michael Wallace II or are used with permission. You may view and share links to this site, but you may not copy, republish, or reuse site content in a way that suggests ownership, endorsement, or affiliation without permission. External Links This site links to external websites and services, including social platforms, portfolio platforms, article platforms, and email providers. Those websites are governed by their own terms and privacy practices. No Warranty This site is provided as-is for general informational and portfolio purposes. I try to keep the content accurate and available, but I do not guarantee that the site will always be error-free, uninterrupted, or current. Changes to These Terms and Policy These terms and this privacy policy may be updated from time to time as the site changes. The effective date above will be updated when material changes are made. Contact Questions about these terms, this privacy policy, or this site's use of information can be sent to hello@janmichael.io.
